title: Acute Left-Sided Diverticulitis
description: Stage with CT, withhold antibiotics when they add nothing, drain large abscesses, pick Hartmann's or primary anastomosis by physiology, and counsel on colonoscopy and elective resection.
objectives: Confirm and stage diverticulitis with contrast-enhanced CT
Omit antibiotics in uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients without systemic inflammation
Treat abscesses by size: antibiotics alone vs percutaneous drainage
Choose between primary anastomosis and Hartmann's procedure by physiology
Know when colonoscopy is and is not needed, and base elective resection on patient factors rather than episode count

references.citation: Sartelli M, Weber DG, Kluger Y, et al. 2020 update of the WSES guidelines for the management of acute colonic diverticulitis in the emergency setting. World J Emerg Surg. 2020;15(1):32.
Peery AF, Shaukat A, Strate LL. AGA clinical practice update on medical management of colonic diverticulitis: expert review. Gastroenterology. 2021;160(3):906-911.e1.

Daniels L, Ünlü Ç, de Korte N, et al. Randomized clinical trial of observational versus antibiotic treatment for a first episode of CT-proven uncomplicated acute diverticulitis. Br J Surg. 2017;104(1):52-61.

Lambrichts DPV, Vennix S, Musters GD, et al. Hartmann's procedure versus sigmoidectomy with primary anastomosis for perforated diverticulitis with purulent or faecal peritonitis (LADIES): a multicentre, parallel-group, randomised, open-label, superiority trial. Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2019;4(8):599-610.
Sawyer RG, Claridge JA, Nathens AB, et al. Trial of short-course antimicrobial therapy for intraabdominal infection. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(21):1996-2005.

start.text: A 61-year-old man, not immunosuppressed and with no significant comorbidity, has 2 days of left lower quadrant pain. Localized LLQ tenderness without peritonism. His last colonoscopy, 2 years ago, was normal.

imaging.text: How do you confirm and stage the diagnosis?

options.label: Plain abdominal films; CT is reserved for surgical candidates
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2B): contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the imaging of first choice in suspected left-sided diverticulitis. An expert ultrasound first, with CT if it is inconclusive or negative, is the accepted alternative.

options.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2B): contrast-enhanced CT is the imaging technique of first choice. The WSES pathway is then keyed to what CT shows: pericolic gas, abscess size, distant free gas, or diffuse fluid.

uncomplicated.text: CT: sigmoid wall thickening with pericolic fat stranding. No abscess, no extraluminal air. He is afebrile, tolerating fluids, and his pain is controlled on oral analgesia. How do you treat him?

options.label: Admit for IV antibiotics; all diverticulitis needs antibiotics
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (strong, 1A): in immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis and no signs of systemic inflammation, do not prescribe antibiotics. In DIABOLO, observation did not prolong recovery and shortened stay (2 vs 3 days).

options.label: No antibiotics: oral analgesia and fluids as an outpatient, with re-evaluation within 7 days
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (1A): no antibiotics for uncomplicated diverticulitis in immunocompetent patients without systemic inflammation, and outpatient care with re-evaluation within 7 days is suggested. AGA 2021: use antibiotics selectively, not routinely, in immunocompetent patients, and strongly advise them in the immunocompromised.

uncomplicated_colonoscopy.text: Six weeks later he is well. His last colonoscopy, 2 years ago, was normal. Does he need colonoscopy now?

options.label: Not routinely: CT-proven uncomplicated disease with a recent normal colonoscopy
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (2B): routine colonic evaluation is not recommended after CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis managed non-operatively. AGA 2021: the decision depends on the patient's history, most recent colonoscopy, and disease severity and course.

options.label: Yes: every episode of diverticulitis mandates colonoscopy
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (2B) does not recommend routine colonoscopy after CT-proven uncomplicated diverticulitis. AGA 2021 individualizes it by history, last colonoscopy, and severity. The decision here rests on his history, his normal colonoscopy 2 years ago, and a mild course.

abscess.text: CT: a 6 cm pericolic abscess with a safe percutaneous window, no free air. He is febrile but hemodynamically stable. How do you treat him?

options.label: IV antibiotics plus CT-guided percutaneous drainage
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): treat large abscesses (over 4–5 cm) with percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics. Small abscesses (under 4–5 cm) get an initial trial of antibiotics alone.

options.label: IV antibiotics alone; any size of abscess will resolve
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (2C): antibiotics alone are for small abscesses (under 4–5 cm). At 6 cm this abscess needs percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics.

options.label: Emergency sigmoid colectomy
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): large abscesses are treated with percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics. An operation is the alternative only when drainage is not feasible or not available.

abscess_colonoscopy.text: The drain is removed and he recovers. What follow-up does he need?

options.label: No colonic evaluation; he had a normal colonoscopy 2 years ago
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): after a diverticular abscess treated non-operatively, plan early colonic evaluation at 4–6 weeks, because a localized colonic abscess can be the presentation of an occult colon cancer. AGA 2021: rarely, a colon malignancy is misdiagnosed as diverticulitis.

options.label: Colonoscopy in 4–6 weeks to exclude malignancy
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2C): after a diverticular abscess treated non-operatively, plan early colonic evaluation at 4–6 weeks. AGA 2021: a colon cancer is rarely misdiagnosed as diverticulitis.

elective.text: He asks whether he should have his sigmoid colon removed to prevent another attack. How do you decide?

options.label: Base the discussion on his symptoms, severity, risks, and preferences, not on the number of episodes
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (2D): plan elective resection on patient-related factors, not on the number of previous episodes. AGA 2021: do not advise elective resection by episode count; personalize it to severity, preferences, risks, and benefits.

options.label: Resection is mandatory after a second episode
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2D) and AGA 2021: elective resection should not be advised based on the number of episodes. Personalize the discussion to disease severity, patient-related factors, preferences, risks, and benefits.

peritonitis.text: CT: free intraperitoneal air and fluid with generalized peritonitis. He is started on broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and resuscitated, and taken to theatre. At laparotomy: purulent peritonitis from a perforated sigmoid (Hinchey III), no fecal contamination.

stable_peritonitis.text: After resuscitation he is hemodynamically stable off vasopressors, immunocompetent, with no major comorbidity. What operation?

options.label: Laparoscopic lavage and drainage without resection as first-line
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (2A): laparoscopic peritoneal lavage is only for very selected patients and is not first-line treatment for peritonitis from diverticulitis.

options.label: Hartmann's procedure
options.feedback: In a stable patient without comorbidity, WSES 2020 (2B) suggests primary resection with anastomosis, with or without a diverting stoma. LADIES: 12-month stoma-free survival was 94.6% after primary anastomosis vs 71.7% after Hartmann's, with no difference in short-term morbidity or mortality.

options.label: Sigmoid resection with primary anastomosis, with or without a diverting loop ileostomy
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2B): in clinically stable patients without comorbidity, primary resection with anastomosis with or without a diverting stoma. LADIES: stoma-free survival at 12 months was 94.6% vs 71.7% with Hartmann's, with similar short-term morbidity and mortality.

shocked_peritonitis.text: Despite resuscitation he is in septic shock on norepinephrine 0.2 µg/kg/min, with a lactate of 5.1 mmol/L. What operation?

options.label: Hartmann's procedure, or damage-control resection with delayed reconstruction
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (strong, 2B): Hartmann's procedure for diffuse peritonitis in critically ill patients and in selected patients with multiple comorbidities. Damage-control surgery with staged laparotomies is suggested in selected unstable patients (weak, 2C).

options.label: Resection with primary anastomosis and no stoma
options.feedback: WSES 2020 recommends Hartmann's procedure for diffuse peritonitis in critically ill patients (strong, 2B), or staged damage-control surgery (2C). Primary anastomosis is suggested for clinically stable patients, the population in which LADIES showed its benefit.

postop_antibiotics.text: Source control has been achieved. How long do antibiotics continue?

options.label: About 4 days after source control
options.feedback: WSES 2020 (weak, 2B): a 4-day postoperative course when source control is adequate. In STOP-IT, about 4 days of fixed therapy gave outcomes similar to about 8 days.

options.label: Two weeks, until all inflammatory markers are normal
options.feedback: With adequate source control, WSES 2020 suggests a 4-day course (2B). In STOP-IT, continuing antibiotics until physiology normalized (median 8 days) gave no better outcomes than about 4 days of fixed therapy.

fail_overtreatment.text: Guideline Deviation: Routine antibiotics and admission for uncomplicated diverticulitis.

fail_abscess.text: Complication: Undrained abscess progressing to sepsis.

fail_emergency_resection.text: Management Error: Emergency resection for a drainable abscess.

fail_missed_cancer.text: Diagnostic Risk: Possible colorectal cancer missed after a complicated episode.

fail_elective.text: Guideline Deviation: Elective resection offered by episode count alone.

fail_lavage.text: Guideline Deviation: Lavage as first-line treatment for generalized peritonitis.

fail_hartmann.text: Guideline Deviation: Hartmann's in a patient suited to primary anastomosis.

fail_leak.text: Complication: Anastomotic leak after primary anastomosis in septic shock.

fail_duration.text: Guideline Deviation: Prolonged antibiotics after source control.

success_nonoperative.text: Managed: Guideline-concordant non-operative care and follow-up.

success_operative.text: Procedure Complete: Source control matched to physiology.
